week.t: NASA sets the Dragon cargo ship’s departure from the station: undock Wed 18 Nov 11:05 am US Eastern, just after midnight in Singapore
NASA Earth Observatory: an astronaut photo of lightning in thunderstorm tops near Borneo, with Singapore’s lights at the edge of the frame
NASA: the Terra satellite, launched in 1999 for a six-year job, stops collecting science data on 1 December after 27 years
Perseverance finds bright rocks rich in hydrated silica at ‘Idubi’, outside Jezero crater
Quanta: the Dark Energy Survey’s final results, 758 nights and a 570-megapixel camera, do not quite fit the standard model of the cosmos
India commits more than €7 million over five years to two new beamlines at the Elettra synchrotron in Trieste, Italy

tiles.cap: Just after midnight tonight, a Dragon carrying frozen science lets go of the station
tiles.nums: US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, 12:05 am Thursday in Singapore: the planned undocking time, weather permitting
tiles.p1: NASA has finally posted the time. SpaceX’s 35th cargo Dragon is to undock from the space-facing port of the station’s Harmony module no earlier than 11:05 am US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, which is 12:05 am on Thursday in Singapore, with NASA’s live coverage starting at 10:45 am Eastern (11:45 pm Singapore). The command comes from SpaceX’s control room in Hawthorne, California, not from the crew. Splashdown off the coast of California is planned for no earlier than 1:50 am Eastern on Thursday 19 November, 2:50 pm Singapore time, and NASA says it will not stream the splashdown itself.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: this Dragon arrived on 15 October with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and experiments. It goes back down with thousands of pounds of cargo, including science samples that were frozen in orbit.
deep: What is in the freezers

NASA lists a 3D-bioprinted blood-vessel construct, built to probe how blood vessels age; frozen tumour organoids that were treated aboard the station, for research into improving cancer treatments; frozen microbe samples from research into how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive, adapt and evolve in space; and a lighting system coming home after more than three years, tested for its effect on astronauts’ sleep.
The last days of packing

NASA’s station blog for Monday and Tuesday describes Anil Menon and Canada’s Joshua Kutryk moving finished samples from the station’s science freezers into portable freezers and stowing them in Dragon, while Luke Delaney, Menon and Jessica Watkins loaded science hardware. Kutryk also processed bacterial colonies for DNA extraction for the antibiotic-resistance work.
Why the ground does it

Dragon is a cargo version with no crew aboard, so SpaceX controllers in Hawthorne send the undock command and fly the departure. It splashes down in the Pacific off the California coast, where NASA and SpaceX teams recover the capsule and its payloads.
The picture
An earlier cargo Dragon (NASA’s caption says the 34th resupply mission) departing after undocking from Harmony’s forward port, photographed by NASA astronaut Jessica Meir. Credit NASA/Jessica Meir.
tiles.src: NASA media advisory M26-087, NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure, 17 Nov 2026 · NASA space station blog, 16 and 17 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia)

tiles.cap: At 6:16 pm Singapore time today, Voyager 1 is one light-day from Earth: 25.902 billion km
tiles.nums: is how long light leaving Earth at 6:16 pm today takes to reach Voyager 1, 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion km) away
tiles.p1: Today, Wednesday 18 November, at 5:16:07 am US Eastern, 6:16:07 pm in Singapore, NASA’s Voyager 1 is 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 km) from Earth, the distance light travels in 24 hours. NASA says no other human-made object has ever been that far away. Last night, after sunset on Tuesday, NASA asked people everywhere to flash V-G-R, Voyager’s call sign, at the sky in Morse code, by phone, torch or glow stick, for its Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day event.
tiles.p2: Why now: Voyager 1 left Earth on 5 September 1977, so the milestone comes 49 years, two months and 11 days after launch. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in November 2035.
deep: How far a light-day is

NASA’s page lists the light-times for comparison: the Moon about 1.3 seconds away, the Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds, Mars 3 to 22 minutes depending on where the two planets are, Neptune four hours and ten minutes, Proxima Centauri about 4.24 light-years. NASA’s page gives Voyager 1’s speed as nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), though a caption on the same page says around 35,000 mph.
The code

V is · · · —, G is — — ·, R is · — ·. NASA’s timing: a dot under one second, a dash about one second, a brief pause between the symbols of a letter and a second or more between letters, repeated for about a minute. Any light does: torch, glow stick, solar lantern, bike light or phone.
Thursday’s panel

A panel at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Thursday 19 November at 12 pm US Eastern, Friday 20 November at 1 am in Singapore, can be watched online on NASA’s site; participants include Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager, and Linda Spilker, the project scientist. NASA says a Voyager documentary is planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
The picture
An artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft, credit NASA/JPL-Caltech.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now? (updated 16 Nov 2026) · Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day? (updated 12 Nov 2026) · Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day · NASA advisory M26-086, 10 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov

tiles.cap: Lightning inside storm tops near Borneo, shot from orbit. Singapore glows at the left
tiles.nums: lightning flashes per second, roughly, across the whole Earth: about 2,000 thunderstorms at any moment and some 5 million flashes a day, by NASA’s estimate
tiles.p1: On 28 October at 14:20 UTC, 10:20 pm in Singapore, a crew member on the space station pointed a Nikon Z9 with a 14 mm lens at the South China Sea near Borneo. The frame, published by NASA’s Earth Observatory on Tuesday, shows several dome-like ‘overshooting tops’ rising out of thunderstorms, two of them lit from inside by lightning. On the left of the picture sit the lights of Singapore, home to 6.2 million people, separated from Indonesia’s Batam and Bintan islands by the Singapore Strait.
tiles.p2: Why here: this is what the afternoon storms in NEA’s forecast look like from orbit. The blue lights west of Singapore are probably fishing fleets using bright lamps to attract squid or small fish; scattered orange points offshore to the northwest are likely gas flares.
deep: What an overshooting top is

A thunderstorm normally spreads out into a flat anvil where it hits the stable air above. When the updraught is strong enough, a dome punches through the anvil, sometimes into the stratosphere. Those domes are the overshooting tops, and they are a sign of a violent updraught beneath.
Lightning from above

Sally Ride wrote that on Earth people see lightning from below the clouds, and in orbit you see it from above. NASA astronaut Anil Menon, on the station now, posted that lightning is his favourite sight from space, ‘like fireflies in the night’.
Try it

The next evening storm, count the seconds between the flash and the thunder and divide by three for the rough distance in kilometres. From the station there is no thunder to hear, only the flashes lighting the clouds from inside.
The picture

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951, taken on 28 October 2026 by an Expedition 75 crew member, provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Tossing Fireworks from Cloud to Cloud, 17 Nov 2026 (Adam Voiland)

tiles.cap: Perseverance has rolled up to ghostly pale rocks on Mars: silica that once soaked in water
tiles.nums: the Martian day, 29 October 2026, on which Perseverance’s Mastcam-Z photographed the bright rocks at ‘Idubi’
tiles.p1: The rover is now outside Jezero crater, in a stretch of ancient Martian crust the team calls the Lac de Charmes region. At a spot named Idubi it found a cluster of rocks far brighter than the volcanic and impact rocks it had been looking at. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument say they are not igneous at all: they are rich in hydrated silica, a water-bearing form of the mineral that makes up quartz and glass.
tiles.p2: Why that matters: on Earth, hydrated silica forms in hydrothermal (hot-water) systems, in soils and in groundwater, and it is good at preserving microfossils. A detailed close-up campaign at Idubi is already under way.
deep: Seen before, but too small
Silica-rich rocks turned up earlier on the inner rim of Jezero crater, but those were too small for the rover’s arm-mounted instruments to examine up close. Idubi offers bigger targets.
Where Idubi is

Perseverance left Jezero crater, where it landed in 2021, and is now on the ancient crust outside the rim, in the region the team calls Lac de Charmes. The post is written by Candice Bedford, a research scientist at Purdue University on the rover team.
The picture
Taken by the left Mastcam-Z camera on 29 October 2026 (Sol 2023) at 13:03 local Mars time. A close-up came from the WATSON camera on the arm the same afternoon. Credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’, 16 Nov 2026 (Candice Bedford, Purdue University)

tiles.cap: A 570-megapixel camera watched the sky for 758 nights. Its final answer does not quite fit
tiles.nums: the strength of the Dark Energy Survey’s hint that dark energy is weakening over time; physicists want 5 sigma before calling anything a discovery
tiles.p1: The Dark Energy Survey began in 2003 with physicists at Fermilab and grew to more than 400 scientists in seven countries. Its tool was the Dark Energy Camera, 570 megapixels, mounted on the 4-metre Victor M. Blanco Telescope at Cerro Tololo in the Chilean Andes. It observed on 758 nights between 2013 and 2019, and in May 2026 released results from its full dataset: thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies. Quanta reported this week that the numbers show a three-sigma preference for dark energy getting weaker, which the standard model of cosmology says should not happen.
tiles.p2: Why now: the DESI survey in Arizona has reported similar misfits since 2024 and runs until at least 2028, and the Rubin Observatory, about six miles from Cerro Tololo, began its survey this year and is expected to see roughly 10 billion galaxies.
deep: The model under strain

Lambda-CDM says the universe is about 30 percent matter, mostly cold dark matter, and 70 percent dark energy, with dark energy constant. Simone Ferraro of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, who is not part of DES, told Quanta ‘there appear to be cracks in that model’ and that the result is ‘enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited’.
Why three sigma is not enough

Three sigma means a fluke of this size would happen by chance only a few times in a thousand, but with many surveys and many ways to slice the data, flukes of that size do turn up. Five sigma, the bar for discovery, is about one chance in a few million.
Back to 1998

The accelerating universe was announced in early 1998 by two teams; Quanta notes the Blanco telescope is famous for its role in that discovery. Joshua Frieman, a DES co-founder, had planned a ‘missing energy’ workshop in 1997; afterwards, he told Quanta, ‘suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop’.
The picture
The 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-metre telescope at Cerro Tololo. Credit Dark Energy Survey / DOE / FNAL / DECam / CTIO / NOIRLab / NSF / AURA.
tiles.src: Quanta Magazine, What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing, 16 Nov 2026 (Charlie Wood; corrected 17 Nov)
tiles.credit: Photo: Dark Energy Survey / DOE / FNAL / DECam / CTIO / NOIRLab / NSF / AURA

tiles.cap: Built for six years, Terra watched Earth for 27. On 1 December its instruments go quiet
tiles.nums: its design life: launched in December 1999 for a six-year mission, Terra stops collecting science data on 1 December 2026
tiles.p1: NASA announced on Tuesday that Terra, the Earth-observing satellite launched in December 1999, will stop collecting science data on 1 December and be switched off completely in January 2027. Its five instruments, MODIS, ASTER, CERES, MISR and MOPITT, have tracked land use, wildfires, dust and smoke, the atmosphere’s composition and ice cover for 27 years, more than four times the six years it was designed for.
tiles.p2: Why now: the satellite’s systems are ageing and its orbit has drifted. MOPITT and parts of CERES and ASTER had already been shut off to save power. The remaining fuel will be used to lower the orbit before the lights go out.
deep: What stays
Everything Terra ever measured stays free and publicly available, NASA says: 27 years of records of land use, wildfires, dust and smoke, atmospheric composition and ice cover.
Why now

NASA gives two reasons for ending now: the satellite’s systems are ageing and its orbit is drifting. The remaining fuel will be used to lower the orbit before the spacecraft is powered off in January 2027.
The picture
Technicians preparing Terra for encapsulation in its rocket fairing before the December 1999 launch. Credit NASA.
tiles.src: NASA Science, NASA’s Terra Mission to End, 17 Nov 2026 (Kate Ramsayer)

tiles.cap: India commits €7 million+ to two beamlines on an Italian synchrotron it has used since ’98
tiles.nums: experiment proposals from Indian groups at Elettra, Trieste, making India the ring’s second-largest user after Italy
tiles.p1: On Friday 13 November, India’s minister of state for science and technology, Jitendra Singh visited Elettra Sincrotrone Trieste in Italy and committed more than €7 million over five years, starting 2026–27, to the Elettra 2.0 upgrade. A synchrotron is a ring in which electrons race at close to the speed of light; where magnets bend them they throw off intense X-rays and ultraviolet, which are piped down ‘beamlines’ to experiments. Indian scientists have used Elettra since 1998, and about 50 to 60 of them travel to Trieste each year.
tiles.p2: Why now: the two existing India-centric beamlines, XRD2 and Xpress, which India helped build for about ₹22 crore and which opened on 20 October 2016, will be decommissioned and replaced by two new ones.
deep: The two new beamlines

Micro-XRD (μXRD) is a microfocus beamline for macromolecular crystallography, working out the shapes of proteins from tiny crystals. Xpress Superbend (Xpress-SB) is for high-pressure diffraction, squeezing samples to see how their atomic structure changes under pressure.
Who uses it

The release says Indian groups have submitted more than 1,100 experimental proposals over the years, second only to Italy’s 54,140 and just ahead of France’s 1,098. The upgraded beamlines are aimed at chemistry, physics, advanced materials and structural biology.
A 25-year partnership

The release counts the relationship from 1998, more than 25 years. India’s Department of Science and Technology has kept it funded: a 2022–2024 programme put ₹2 crore over three years into sending 50 Indian researchers a year to Trieste, and ₹1.5 crore is proposed for 2025–2027. The minister signed a letter of intent for the new beamlines during the visit.
The picture
An uncaptioned image from the Press Information Bureau release of 14 November 2026. Credit PIB.
tiles.src: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Science & Technology: India commits over 7 million Euros as co-partner in Elettra 2.0 in Italy for development of next-generation synchrotron beamlines, 14 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: Press Information Bureau, Government of India

tiles.cap: A grape runs away from a magnet. Both poles. Try it with a neodymium magnet and a straw
tiles.nums: to a million times weaker than the pull of a magnet on iron: the repulsion a strong magnet exerts on water, and so on a grape
tiles.p1: Slide two big grapes onto the ends of a drinking straw, hang the straw from a 60 cm thread so it can turn freely, and let it settle. Bring one pole of a strong neodymium magnet close to a grape without touching it. The grape drifts away. Let it stop, flip the magnet to the other pole, and it drifts away again. Iron would have jumped onto the magnet; the grape is repelled by both poles.
tiles.p2: Why: a grape is mostly water, and water is diamagnetic. Every electron in it is paired with a partner spinning the opposite way, so there is no built-in magnetism to attract. Instead the approaching magnet induces tiny currents in the atoms, and by Lenz’s law those currents push back.
deep: Three kinds of magnetic

Ferromagnets, iron, nickel and cobalt, have unpaired electrons that line up in domains and pull hard. Paramagnets like aluminium and liquid oxygen are weakly attracted. Diamagnets, helium, bismuth, graphite, water, are weakly repelled. The Exploratorium puts the diamagnetic push at roughly 100,000 to 1,000,000 times weaker than ferromagnetism, which is why you need a rare-earth magnet and a near-frictionless hanging straw to see it. Feynman puts ordinary magnetic effects at a thousand to a million times smaller than ferromagnetism.
Why it works at all

In Feynman’s Lectures the chapter on the magnetism of matter shows that diamagnetism does not depend on temperature while paramagnetism gets stronger as things get colder, and that classical physics on its own cannot produce either effect; it takes quantum mechanics to explain why atoms respond the way they do.
Go further

Swap the grapes for aluminium foil balls, wood, or prunes and see which, if any, move. Watch out: the Exploratorium warns that neodymium magnets this size give a painful pinch if skin is caught between two of them.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, Magnetic Fruit · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, Ch. 34, The Magnetism of Matter

tiles.cap: A single molecule’s spin, read out with light, flips in under 50 ns and holds for 2.2 ms
tiles.nums: spin coherence time of a single-molecule qubit at 4.5 K; a flip takes under 50 ns, so thousands of operations fit in one coherence window
tiles.p1: A qubit is a quantum bit, something that can hold a 0, a 1 or a blend of the two. Physics World reported on Tuesday that NVision Quantum Technologies in Ulm, Germany, co-founded by Martin Plenio of Ulm University, has switched on, controlled and read out the spin of individual molecules using light and microwaves, at 4.5 K, a little above absolute zero. The spin stayed coherent for 2.2 milliseconds and relaxed in 21 ms; a flip took under 50 nanoseconds. The work is published in Nature.
tiles.p2: Do the sum: 2.2 ms is 2,200,000 ns. Divided by 50 ns per flip, that is 44,000 flips before the spin forgets itself; Physics World reckons this allows ‘as many as thousands’ of operations per coherence window.
deep: Why light

The molecule’s spin transitions are separated by at least 1.555 GHz, allowing clean optical readout. The company, with the US photonic-chip maker HyperLight, hopes to put the molecules on integrated photonic chips; its stated goal is 1,000 fault-tolerant qubits by 2030, with the first prototype chips by the end of 2026.
Coherence vs relaxation

Relaxation (21 ms) is how long the spin takes to fall back to its lowest state. Coherence (2.2 ms) is how long its quantum phase stays well defined, which is what computation needs. Coherence is usually the shorter and harder number.
What 4.5 K means
4.5 kelvin is about −268.7 °C, just above the 4.2 K at which helium boils. At that temperature the molecule’s surroundings barely jostle it, which is why the spin can hold still for milliseconds.
tiles.src: Physics World, Single-molecule spin qubits can be controlled with light, 17 Nov 2026 (Isabelle Dumé) · Nature, Schwartz, Pfender, Roggors et al. 2026 (doi 10.1038/s41586-026-11147-6)

tiles.cap: Google’s glasses: a 12 MP camera, 41 g, nine hours, no screen. A reviewer heard them leak
tiles.nums: the weight of Google’s new camera-and-speaker glasses, which Google puts at around 41 grams; nine hours of battery, seven recharges from the case
tiles.p1: Google opened pre-orders on 12 November for ‘intelligent eyewear’ engineered by Samsung and sold as Warby Parker frames from $395 and Gentle Monster frames from $449, on sale in stores and online from 10 December in the US and South Korea. Inside each pair: one 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera with HDR and stabilisation, open-ear speakers, microphones that talk to Gemini, and a battery Google rates at up to nine hours, with a case that recharges the frames up to seven times. There is no display: you hear answers, you do not see them. Weight is around 41 grams.
tiles.p2: What Tom’s Guide found: Kate Kozuch tried them at a Google demonstration this month and liked that they feel like eyewear rather than a gadget, but noticed a delay in live translation, sound leaking to people nearby at higher volumes, photos that are only ‘okay’, and a battery figure that heavy camera use will surely cut.
deep: The privacy engineering

A privacy LED lights when the camera is on, and Google says recording is designed to stop if the light is covered or disabled. There is a physical off switch. Bystanders’ faces are blurred before images reach Gemini, and Google says camera images are not saved to Gemini history or used for training or ads. Kozuch’s point: the same design that makes the wearer comfortable ‘could make it harder for someone else to recognize that recording is possible’, and how the protections work in real use is one of the things she lists as ‘unresolved’.
What it does

Live translation across more than 70 languages, turn-by-turn Maps directions spoken through the open-ear speakers, and a Gemini that can see what you see and keep answering follow-ups without a wake word. Taps and swipes on the right side of the frame control music; a physical button takes the picture. You need a Pixel 7 or newer, a recent Galaxy, or an iPhone 13 Pro or newer, and an account for ages 18 and up.
What the prototype had that this does not

At Google I/O in May, Tom’s Guide’s Jason England tried the software on a prototype with a monocular waveguide display, though reporters could not wear the glasses themselves. He reported then that the first glasses would all be display-free, and they are.
tiles.src: Google, The Keyword: Google intelligent eyewear collections now available for pre-order, 12 Nov 2026 · Tom’s Guide, Kate Kozuch, 12 Nov 2026 · Tom’s Guide, Jason England, 20 May 2026

tiles.cap: TCL claims 10,000 nits for its X11L TV. A lab got 2,679, yet crowned it king of colour
tiles.nums: local dimming zones, at most, behind TCL’s X11L (the 98-inch; the 75-inch has 14,400), each a patch of mini-LEDs that can go dark on its own
tiles.p1: TIME put TCL’s X11L on its 2026 Best Inventions list for its ‘SQD’, super quantum dot, backlight: quantum dots that emit light at ‘more specific nanometer wavelengths than previously available tech’, which TIME says makes the picture both very colour-accurate and very bright. The 75, 85 and 98-inch sets use up to 20,736 dimming zones, a native 144 Hz panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ and a Bang & Olufsen sound system. The 85-inch weighs 112.9 lb (51 kg) without its stand.
tiles.p2: What the lab said: Tom’s Guide’s Kate Kozuch measured 2,679 nits of HDR brightness on a 10 percent window against the ‘up to 10,000 peak nits’ on TCL’s spec sheet, and 91.77 percent of the Rec.2020 colour space against the claimed 100. Even so, she called it one of the brightest Mini-LED TVs you can buy and ‘the new king of color’.
deep: Why the gap in nits

Tom’s Guide says TCL ‘made some bold claims about the X11L’s color and brightness capabilities, and while our testing doesn’t quite meet those claims, it still paints a very positive picture’. A 10 percent window is the standard test the site uses for every set. For scale, its numbers for rivals were 3,332 nits for TCL’s own 2025 QM8K, 2,713 for Sony’s Bravia 9 and 2,109 for Samsung’s QN90F. Input lag measured 11.7 ms.
What reviewers found wrong

Extremely expensive at launch: $6,999 for 75 inches, $7,999 for 85 and $9,999 for 98 (TCL’s US site now lists them at $2,999.99, $4,999.99 and $6,999.99). Motion is ‘not class-leading’, with some smearing in fast action. The wide-set feet need a very large stand. The sound is a plus, ‘strong volume and decent clarity’, good enough that many buyers could skip a soundbar.
Quantum dots in one line

A quantum dot is a crystal a few nanometres across; the smaller the dot, the bluer the light it gives off when excited. Shrink or grow them precisely and you tune the colour, which is what SQD claims to do better than before.
tiles.src: TIME, Best Inventions 2026: TCL X11L SQD-Mini LED TV (Justin Pot, 15 Oct 2026) · TCL US spec page, X11L series · Tom’s Guide review, Kate Kozuch, 20 Feb 2026 · Notebookcheck CES report (zone counts by size)

tiles.cap: Northeast Monsoon setting in: 32–34 °C, afternoon storms. Paya Lebar hit 35.4 °C on 4 Nov
tiles.nums: of rain fell around Rivervale Drive on 6 November, the biggest daily total of the first half of the month
tiles.p1: NEA’s outlook for the rest of November, issued Monday 16 November, says Northeast Monsoon conditions are expected to set in over Singapore in the second half of the month as the prevailing winds strengthen and shift to blow from the northeast or northwest. Expect short thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days, running into the night on a few days; on some days the showers could be widespread and heavy. Daily highs of 32 to 34 °C, slightly above 34 on a few days; around 23 °C on some rainy days.
tiles.p2: Looking back at 1–15 November: 35.4 °C at Paya Lebar on 4 November, the month’s high so far, and daily maxima above 34 °C on seven occasions.
deep: Uneven rain

About half the island had above-average rain in the first half of November. Somerset was 44 percent above its average; Tanjong Katong 65 percent below. Total rainfall for the second half is forecast to be slightly above the long-term average over most of the island.
6 November
Widespread moderate to heavy thundery showers; 94.2 mm around Rivervale Drive that day, the highest daily total of the fortnight.
Today
The 24-hour forecast for Wednesday 18 November: thundery showers over many areas in the afternoon, 24 to 33 °C, humidity 60 to 95 percent, variable winds of 5 to 15 km/h.
The picture
The image from NEA’s outlook page of 16 November 2026. Credit NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore.
tiles.src: NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore, Wet Weather To Continue For Rest Of November 2026 With Onset Of Northeast Monsoon, 16 Nov 2026 · weather.gov.sg 24-hour forecast, 18 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: 74 dengue cases last week, up 20 on the week before, and eight active clusters
tiles.nums: dengue cases reported in the week ending Saturday 14 November, an increase of 20 from the previous week; eight active clusters as of 16 November
tiles.p1: NEA’s dengue page, updated on Tuesday 17 November, counts 74 cases in the week ending 14 November, up from 54 the week before. Eight clusters were active as of 16 November. NEA’s daily table shows 8, 15, 11, 9 and 20 cases from Tuesday 10 to Saturday 14 November, then 10 on Sunday 15 November; Saturday 14 November alone had 20 cases, the busiest day in the table. The 2026 total after 45 weeks stands at 2,960.
tiles.p2: Why now: the wet weeks ahead in NEA’s outlook mean more standing water, and the Aedes mosquito that carries dengue breeds in small containers of stagnant water.
deep: The last six weeks
Weekly cases since early October: 79, 60, 61, 68, 54, 74. Flat to falling until the latest week. The first two days of the current week, 15 and 16 November, logged 12 by 11 am on Monday.
Reading a weekly count

NEA’s ‘E-week’ runs from Sunday midnight to Saturday night. NEA notes that day-to-day numbers fluctuate with how many cases are notified each day, so weekly numbers are a better reflection of actual trends. It also publishes the cluster count, eight as of 16 November.
What you can check
Walk round the block after a storm and count containers holding water: plant saucers, drain gullies, a bin lid. Each one is a possible breeding site.
tiles.src: NEA, Dengue cases (weekly and daily tables), last updated 17 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A finless paper rocket spirals and tumbles. Add four fins at 90° and it flies straight
tiles.nums: apart: bend four triangular fins into a + shape at the open end of the tube and the rocket stops spiralling
tiles.p1: Cut a sheet of paper in half both ways to get four rectangles. Wrap one tightly round a pencil to make a tube, tape it, slide the pencil out, then pinch and tape one end shut for the nose. Slide the tube over a drinking straw, take a deep breath and blow. Measure where it lands. It flies straight for a moment, then spirals out of control and tumbles.
tiles.p2: Now the fix: cut two right-angled triangles with long sides of about 8 cm. On each, draw a line from the right angle to the middle of the long side, add two parallel lines about 5 mm either side of it, and fold along those two lines so two fins stand up with a flat strip between them. Tape both to the open end so you have four fins, and bend the fins into a + shape, 90 degrees apart. Launch again and measure.
deep: Why fins work

Fins put the centre of pressure, the point where the air’s push acts, behind the centre of mass. Any wobble then tilts the fins into the airflow, and the air pushes them back in line. Rockets and missiles usually carry triangular fins at their bases for exactly this reason, and arrows need the same kind of stability.
Make it an experiment

Change one thing at a time: two fins against four, half-moon fins against triangles, fins in the middle of the body or up near the nose. Launch each design several times and record every distance, because one blow is never the same as the next.
Who wrote it

The procedure comes from Science Buddies via Science News Explores, published Tuesday 17 November. It wants a windless space and, if you want numbers, a measuring tape; nothing else you do not already have at home.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, Experiment: Construct and test paper rockets, 17 Nov 2026 (Science Buddies)

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, doing 48% better on the problems. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: the paper’s own explanation is that students ‘attempt to use GPT-4 as a crutch’ during the problem sessions, so they never build the skill themselves.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, different result.
What the researchers concluded
The paper’s worry is that students use a plain chatbot ‘as a crutch’. The hint-only tutor, designed to guide students instead of directly giving answers, avoided the damage.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later.
tiles.src: PNAS, 25 Jun 2025, Bastani et al.: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (doi 10.1073/pnas.2422633122)

tiles.cap: The 2016 Mirai worm was a few kilobytes. The AI worms two teams built: tens of gigabytes
tiles.nums: Android smart TVs networked together to host one test worm: it ran thousands of times more slowly than on GPU computers
tiles.p1: A computer worm is a program that copies itself from machine to machine without anyone clicking. Science News reported on Monday that two separate teams have shown an attacker could turn an AI model into a worm that spreads and adapts on its own. Jonas Guan, an AI researcher at the University of Toronto, and colleagues posted a preprint on arXiv on 2 June describing an ‘octopus-style’ worm; AI company Anthropic posted a report on 12 October describing a ‘digital slime mould’. Guan’s team kept its worm off the real internet and, he says, spent considerable effort making sure it could not escape the lab.
tiles.p2: Why it is not here yet: Mirai, the worm that took down Reddit and Spotify in 2016 after spreading by guessing default passwords on hundreds of thousands of routers, security cameras and baby monitors, was a few kilobytes. These AI models are tens of gigabytes, and on 15 networked smart TVs one ran thousands of times slower than on proper GPUs.
deep: What the tests showed

Guan’s worm, in a virtual network of GPU machines and simulated office printers and security cameras, found a way to survive a reboot without being asked to. Anthropic’s separate GPU experiment showed its worm adapting attacks to different kinds of device. Michael Alexander Riegler of the Simula Metropolitan Center in Oslo, not involved in either, notes both test networks made spreading easier than the real world would.
How Mirai was stopped

Rebooting cleared it, and changing the default username and password stopped reinfection. Zane Ma of Oregon State University, who analysed Mirai, says ‘just using this very simple technique’ it infected hundreds of thousands of devices. Riegler says strong passwords and regular updates would have stopped both of the demonstrated attacks.
How close

Anthropic estimates AI worms are months away; Riegler and Guan think longer. ‘The ingredients are converging,’ Riegler says. Guan’s team is building an AI defender and says it is ‘working on the problem day and night’. Zane Ma says internet providers can spot the unusual traffic a worm makes and quarantine the infected devices by cutting them off.
tiles.src: Science News, We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?, 16 Nov 2026 (Kathryn Hulick)
